title: Not beyond what you can bear
hook: Allah burdens no soul beyond its capacity, our Lord, forgive us (2:286)
carry: not beyond what I can bear

segments.voice: Yesterday: kitab, the long verse on debts, and your line, lend and write. Today, the last verse of al-Baqarah.

Al-Baqarah is two hundred eighty-six verses long. Laws, stories, warnings, arguments: the cow, Ayat al-Kursi, a man asleep for a hundred years, a debt written down. And at the very end it does something unexpected. It stops talking to people and turns into words people say back. Its last verse is a list of requests, and it opens with a promise about weight.
screen: `286 VERSES.` → `LAWS, STORIES, A DEBT.` → `THE END TURNS INTO A PRAYER.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's translation, the verse opens: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." The Arabic for scope is wus'a, capacity, the room a thing has inside it. Every soul has a size, and what's asked of it fits inside. Then the requests, each starting with our Lord. Don't take us to task if we forget or slip. Don't lay on us a burden like the one laid on those before us. Don't make us carry what we have no strength for. Pardon us, forgive us, have mercy on us. There's a story behind it, in Sahih Muslim. When the verse before, 2:284, came down, saying God will call people to account for what's in their hearts, shown or hidden, the companions were frightened. They came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ on their knees and said this was more than they could carry. He told them to say instead: we hear and we obey. They said it, and then these last two verses came. A related report in the same collection, from Ibn Abbas, says that after each request, God answered: I have done so. A hadith in Bukhari adds that whoever recites these last two verses at night, they will be enough for him; scholars read enough as protection, as a night prayer, or both. So the surah ends where some people end their day, in bed, saying these two verses. It doesn't promise that nothing will be heavy. It says the weight was measured to the one carrying it.
screen: `NOT BEYOND ITS SCOPE: WUS'A, CAPACITY` · `OUR LORD: A LIST OF REQUESTS` · `THE FRIGHTENED COMPANIONS` · `ENOUGH FOR THE NIGHT` · then, large: `ALLAH TASKETH NOT A SOUL BEYOND ITS SCOPE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that feels heavy right now; don't solve it, just notice how big it is, and that you're still here, holding it. On each out-breath, let the line be there: not beyond what I can bear. If you pray, you can add the verse's own words: our Lord, pardon us.
Wus'a. Capacity, the room a soul has inside it — al-Baqarah's closing promise that nothing asked exceeds it. Today's word.
Your line: not beyond what I can bear. In the report, the frightened companions were answered: I have done so. That's al-Baqarah, start to finish.

howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the last two verses of al-Baqarah (2:285–286) every night before sleeping, following a hadith that they suffice whoever reads them at night; the requests of 2:286 are also said often in personal supplication.

original.note: Arabic: God does not burden a soul except to its capacity (2:286).

trapdoor: what you thought: God won't give you more than you can handle.
what it means: what God asks of a soul fits within its capacity, and the verse turns at once into requests for pardon and mercy.
what a scholar hears: wus'a, capacity, a word about room and width; and a report in Sahih Muslim that 2:285–286 came down after 2:284 alarmed the companions.

chat.says: Does the Qur'an say we're never given more than we can carry?
options: 2:286: God doesn't task a soul beyond its scope; the weight fits the carrier.
It says strong believers never feel any burden as heavy at all.
It says burdens are only ever a punishment for what you did wrong.
chat.meaning: Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope (2:286). It doesn't promise nothing is heavy; it says the weight is measured.
